I have sat in a lot of first meetings, and here is what I have learned. When somebody introduces themselves to me, I do not need the history. I need the present. What do you own right now? What problem is on your desk this month? Last year a new controller joined our call from Brazil, and she spent two full minutes on her career. Big Four, three companies, fifteen years. All impressive. But when she finished, I still did not know why she was on the call. So my advice is simple. Start with today. Say what you are responsible for, in one sentence. Then, only if somebody asks, go back and tell them how you got there. The history is your answer to the second question, not the first.

I disagree with that, and I have run finance teams on three continents. When I meet somebody new, especially somebody I will have to trust with numbers, the first thing I want to know is where they learned the job. If you tell me you started at a Big Four firm, I already know how you were trained. I know you have closed a thousand months and survived a thousand audits. That is not history. That is credibility, and it takes you ten seconds to say. So do not skip it. Say where you started, say what you have done since then, and then tell me what you are working on now. People do not follow a job title. They follow a track record.
